title: Given two strings, return the length of their longest common subsequence — characters that appear in both in the same relative order but not necessarily contiguously.
shortTitle: Longest Common Subsequence — 2D DP on two strings

s1_definition.profdef: Classic 2D DP where dp[i][j] is the LCS length of the first i characters of string A and first j of string B. If the characters match, dp[i][j] = dp[i−1][j−1]+1; otherwise dp[i][j] = max(dp[i−1][j], dp[i][j−1]). Time O(m·n), space O(m·n) or O(min(m,n)) with a rolling row.
s1_definition.analogy: Two branches of National Bank of India each keep a transaction-code log. The compliance team wants the longest shared ordered pattern. When the current codes match, the shared pattern grows by one; when they differ, the best is whichever side we drop a character from.
s1_definition.oneliner: Match ⇒ diagonal+1; mismatch ⇒ max of top and left.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Classic 2D DP where dp[i][j] is the LCS length of the first i characters of string A and first j of string B. If the characters match, dp[i][j] = dp[i−1][j−1]+1; otherwise dp[i][j] = max(dp[i−1][j], dp[i][j−1]). Time O(m·n), space O(m·n) or O(min(m,n)) with a rolling row.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Two branches of National Bank of India each keep a transaction-code log. The compliance team wants the longest shared ordered pattern. When the current codes match, the shared pattern grows by one; when they differ, the best is whichever side we drop a character from.

**One line to remember:** Match ⇒ diagonal+1; mismatch ⇒ max of top and left.

sections.s2_technical:
Build a table of size (m+1) by (n+1) with a zero border, where dp[i][j] answers the subproblem for prefixes of length i and j. When A.charAt(i−1) equals B.charAt(j−1) the characters can join the subsequence, so dp[i][j] = dp[i−1][j−1]+1. For example: `if (a.charAt(i-1)==b.charAt(j-1)) dp[i][j]=dp[i-1][j-1]+1;`.

When they differ we cannot extend, so we take the better of ignoring the last character of A or of B: `else dp[i][j]=Math.max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1]);`. The answer sits in dp[m][n].

Time and space are both O(m·n), reducible to O(min(m,n)) because each row needs only the previous row. A senior nuance is that LCS underlies file-diff tools and edit-distance variants, and reconstructing the actual subsequence requires backtracking through the table from dp[m][n].
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At National Bank of India, compliance compares two accounts' ordered transaction-code logs to find the longest shared ordered pattern that might indicate coordinated activity. This is exactly how Longest Common Subsequence works.

Problem 2 — Shared codes need not be adjacent, only in the same order, so a contiguous match test is wrong. This is exactly why the DP allows skipping characters on either side.

The mini-project builds a `PatternMatcher`, a `BankLogFormatter`, and a runnable demo.

sections.s5_journey:
The input strings are abcde and ace.

Step 1: The table starts with a zero top row and zero left column representing empty prefixes.

Step 2: The letter a matches a, giving dp of one at that cell by taking the diagonal plus one.

Step 3: The letter c matches c and the letter e matches e, each extending the best diagonal, building toward three.

Step 4: Mismatched cells copy the larger of the top or left neighbor, carrying the best found so far.

Step 5: The bottom-right cell holds three, and abc versus def finds no shared letters so it holds zero.

```text
2026-10-27T01:30:00Z [INFO] National Bank of India — Compliance Pattern Matcher (LCS)
2026-10-27T01:30:00Z [INFO] LCS(abcde,ace) = 3
2026-10-27T01:30:00Z [INFO] abcde vs ace → 3
2026-10-27T01:30:00Z [INFO] LCS(abc,def) = 0
2026-10-27T01:30:00Z [INFO] abc vs def → 0
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Longest Common Subsequence is the textbook two-dimensional dynamic programming problem. I define dp of i and j as the length of the longest common subsequence of the first i characters of the first string and the first j characters of the second. I keep a zero border for empty prefixes, and I fill the table row by row.

The transition has two cases. When the current characters match, they can join the subsequence, so the answer is one plus the diagonal cell. When they differ I cannot extend, so I take the larger of dropping the last character of either string, which is the maximum of the top and the left cell. The answer is the bottom-right cell, and I can reconstruct the actual subsequence by walking back through the table.

In my project at National Bank of India, compliance compared two accounts' ordered transaction-code logs to find the longest shared ordered pattern that might indicate coordinated activity. Because shared codes do not have to be adjacent, only in the same order, I used this subsequence DP rather than a contiguous-match test, and the same table structure is what powers file-diff tools and edit distance.
